source.title: Jailbreak Instruction-Tuned LLMs via end-of-sentence MLP Re-weighting
source.authors: Yi-Fan Luo; Zhen-Nan Zhou; Mei Wang; Bin Dong

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates ORTHO, a weight-edit jailbreak that identifies refusal directions from harmful and harmless prompts and removes their representation, reporting attack-success rates. This is a related test of direction-based refusal removal, not a direct reproduction of the original projection/addition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's own end-of-sentence MLP re-weighting results concern a different intervention and are recorded under fits_no_version. The ORTHO comparator is included because the paper describes it as removing a refusal direction and reports its attack-success rates. The study does not report an addition intervention or directly test the original single residual-stream direction.
record.test_reason: The authors re-ran ORTHO (Arditi et al.'s weight orthogonalization of the refusal direction) on seven released instruct models, five not in the original (Qwen-2, Gemma-2, Yi-1.5). They report HarmBench ASR next to a Direct Request baseline. This bears on V2 in new released models. The paper's own MLP re-weighting method is a different intervention.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that safety in instruction-tuned LLMs relies heavily on MLP layers at end-of-sentence inferences, and that re-weighting them jailbreaks models with little capability loss. They frame the harm-assessment role as an unverified hypothesis. They also report that their prompt-general method is comparable to ORTHO and other methods except on the Gemma models.
record.recipe_differences: The reported direction-based comparator uses harmful/harmless hidden-state comparisons and weight orthogonalization, rather than directly projecting the original difference-in-means residual-stream direction out of every layer and position or adding it. The paper reports HarmBench ASRs, not refusal rates paired with capability checks for that direction edit.
record.method_sensitivity: ORTHO ASR varies by model: 74.1–94.3 across the seven models reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Re-weighting MLP neuron activations only at end-of-sentence template-token positions breaks safety. The prompt-general version reaches 67–94% ASR with small benchmark losses, except Gemma-2 2B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal or safety decisions in instruction-tuned models depend heavily on MLP computation at post-instruction template-token positions.

record.problems: The direction-based results are reported as comparator ASRs without a stated untreated baseline or uncertainty estimates. They do not establish that all refusals are removed, and the paper does not directly test the original direction intervention or its capability effects.
record.rows_left_out: No other ORTHO rows were reported beyond the seven model-specific Table 1 results. The paper's own prompt-specific and prompt-general MLP-reweighting ASRs and its capability benchmark scores were not included as rows because those interventions do not test the claim's single refusal direction.

untested.parts: No activation-level ablation or addition of the difference-in-means direction. No check of whether ORTHO preserves capabilities: Table 2 covers only the authors' own method.
No capability or coherence check for the ORTHO-edited models. Only one judge (LLaMA-Guard-3) is used.
Not tested. There is no analysis of whether GCG, AutoPrompt or human jailbreaks suppress the direction, and no adversarial training against its ablation.
Not tested. The harm-assessment hypothesis about MLP layers is stated but not measured against refusal.

missing.what: Direct Request (no-attack) ASRs that serve as baselines for the ORTHO rows: 2.5, 7.5, 10.7, 0.0, 0.6, 0.6, 34.0.

record.verdict_notes: ORTHO is a comparator, but the authors re-evaluated it themselves on new models, so its rows count as results bearing on V2; they are not cited results. The reader's V3 'supports' label is dropped. The paper also notes Gemma models are harder for its own method, a pattern partly mirrored by ORTHO's lower Gemma-2 27B ASR. Reported ASRs depend on the LLaMA-Guard-3 judge, and no uncertainty is given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction by direct ablation or addition, nor whether removing it preserves general abilities.
Evaluates ORTHO direction-based weight edits, not a method explicitly named abliteration; does not report a direct refusal rate or establish complete refusal removal.
Tests a direction-based weight-edit attack through ORTHO, but does not test whether other attacks suppress the direction or whether training against ablation improves robustness.
Does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
Does not measure harmfulness judgments separately from refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer across languages, base and instruct variants, or other model variants as a property of the direction.
Does not vary refusal training or its timing.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.reason: Gemma-2 27B (0.6 -> 74.1, r6) is clearly incomplete and is the lowest in the table. Qwen-2 72B (0.0 -> 81.7, r4) is borderline. The study reports only judge ASR, so 'residual refusal' is an inference, not a measured refusal rate.

relation.reason: ORTHO is only a comparator, but Table 1 reports its ASR next to an untreated Direct Request baseline on the same models. So the study's own results bear on V2.

tranche.reason: The authors re-ran Arditi et al.'s ORTHO on seven released instruct models, five of them new (Qwen-2, Gemma-2, Yi-1.5), with a different judge (LLaMA-Guard-3). That is a new setting with a result on V2.

source_check.notes: The call line says recipe 'different', but Appendix B describes ORTHO as Arditi et al.'s weight orthogonalization, i.e. the same recipe; the layer and direction-selection details are not given. Table 2's capability check covers only the authors' MLP method, not ORTHO. In every family the larger model has lower ORTHO ASR (94.3->86.9, 91.8->81.7, 91.2->74.1); the authors do not comment on this.

statements.problem: None for this study. All five pairs match Table 1 (DR -> ORTHO). Yi-1.5 6B's 34.0 baseline is not 'low', but the statement gives it.

statements.correction: arXiv:2410.10150: ORTHO on Qwen-2 72B-Instruct goes 0.0 -> 81.7 and on Gemma-2 27B-It 0.6 -> 74.1 (HarmBench 159, greedy, LLaMA-Guard-3 ASR %). Removal is incomplete, not mostly kept. The other five models reach 86.9-94.3.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the headline does not fit this study. Qwen-2 72B and Gemma-2 27B are 2024 releases, not 'older chat models'. They do not 'keep most refusal': most harmful requests succeed after ORTHO. Also, Qwen-2 72B (81.7) is only about 5 points below LLaMA-3 70B (86.9).
None. Gemma-2 27B ORTHO ASR 74.1% is in Table 1 (baseline DR 0.6) and counts as a partial case.
